topic: The stakeholder group most often omitted from mapping
stem: Discovery teams reliably map the sponsor, the budget holder and the end users. Which group is most often left out, and whose omission most often shows up later as failed adoption?

options.text: The infrastructure team who provision the runtime environment and the network route to the model endpoint.
People whose work the system changes without their using it — reviewers and second-line teams who absorb its output.
The internal communications team who will announce the launch on the staff intranet and in the weekly team briefings.
The model provider's customer success contact, who runs the quarterly service review and the usage report.

explanation.correct: Automation rarely removes work; it moves it. A system that drafts, classifies or triages hands its output to someone who must now check, correct or act on it, often at a volume and cadence they never agreed to. Those people are not users, so they miss the requirements sessions, and they are the ones who quietly route around the system when it lands. Mapping them during discovery surfaces their capacity limits and their quality bar, both of which are design constraints.

distractors.A: Infrastructure teams are usually engaged, because a project cannot deploy without them. Their omission produces a delay, not the pattern of a launched system that nobody uses.
distractors.C: Communications shapes how a launch is described, but a well-announced system that shifts unwanted work onto a reviewing team still fails. Messaging cannot repair a workload the design created.
distractors.D: A supplier relationship, not an internal stakeholder whose behaviour determines adoption. Nothing about the account contact influences whether the affected teams accept the output.

explanation.concept: Map by effect, not by title: for every output the system produces, identify who receives it, what they must now do differently, and whether their capacity and incentives support that. Anyone whose workload or accountability changes is a stakeholder, whether or not they ever open the interface.
explanation.tip: When an item asks who was missed, ignore the people who appear on the project org chart. The answer is almost always the group downstream of the output.

topic: Demand forecasting mis-framed as a language model task
stem: A specialty food distributor asks for Claude to predict next month's order volume for each of 12,000 SKU-and-depot combinations, using four years of transaction history, a promotions calendar, and free-text supplier and account-manager notes. What should discovery conclude?

options.text: Feasible as asked: place the last twenty-four months of history for each SKU-and-depot combination in the prompt and ask for a numeric forecast.
Feasible if the transaction history is indexed for retrieval so each forecast call sees only the relevant SKU-and-depot series and its promotions.
The numeric forecast belongs to a statistical forecaster; the model's work is turning the free-text notes into features and explaining variances.
Feasible only if a model is fine-tuned on the four years of transaction history so that seasonality and promotion lift are learned into the weights.

explanation.correct: The task decomposes, and discovery's job is to make the seam visible. Seasonality, trend and promotion lift over four years of dense numeric series are exactly what forecasting methods are built for: they are cheap at 12,000 series, they produce calibrated intervals, and they can be backtested. The genuinely unstructured input is the note text, which no forecaster can consume. Extracting structured signals from those notes, and narrating why a forecast moved, are the parts that justify a model.

distractors.A: Treats a language model as a numeric extrapolator. Even setting aside quality, 12,000 series each carrying two years of history is a per-cycle cost and latency profile no one would accept for a job a forecaster completes in minutes.
distractors.B: Solves a context-volume problem that only exists because the wrong tool was chosen. Retrieval makes the calls fit; it does nothing to make the arithmetic of extrapolation a language task.
distractors.D: Fine-tuning adapts style and task format, not numeric time-series estimation, and the proposal commits significant cost to reproduce badly what an off-the-shelf forecaster does well. It is the most expensive route to the same wrong architecture.

explanation.concept: Decompose a requested use case before accepting or rejecting it. Numeric prediction over dense structured history is classical modelling; interpretation of free text into features or explanations is model work. Most real requests contain both, and the valuable discovery output is the boundary between them, not a verdict on the whole.
explanation.tip: When a stem lists both a long numeric history and some free-text notes, expect the answer to split the task rather than to accept or reject it wholesale.

topic: Acceptance metric that can be satisfied by the wrong behaviour
stem: A telecommunications provider proposes a single acceptance criterion for its chat assistant pilot: containment rate of at least 60%, where containment means the chat ended without transfer to a human agent. Discovery finds that in 200 transcripts from a vendor demo deployment, 31% of contained chats were followed by the same customer contacting again within 48 hours. What is the most serious defect in this as the sole acceptance criterion?

options.text: Sixty percent is unrealistic for a first pilot and should be reset to the level comparable operator deployments achieve in their first year.
Containment cannot be computed automatically from the chat platform and would need manual review of every transcript, making the criterion impractical.
Containment should be reported per intent, so that chats about intents the assistant was never designed to resolve are removed from the denominator before the 60% target is applied.
Containment counts the absence of a transfer, not whether the problem was solved; it must be paired with a repeat-contact resolution measure.

explanation.correct: The demo figure is the tell: nearly a third of contained chats produced another contact within two days, which means containment and resolution have already come apart in observed data. A metric that rewards not-transferring creates direct pressure toward refusing handoff, and the system will optimise for the measure rather than the outcome. The fix is to define success as resolution — no repeat contact on the same issue inside an agreed window, plus explicit handoff on out-of-scope intents — with containment retained only as a supporting indicator.

distractors.A: Argues about the number when the problem is the quantity being counted. Lowering an unsound target to a more modest unsound target leaves the same incentive intact.
distractors.B: Containment is derivable from transfer events in the chat platform's own logs. Measurability is not the issue here; what the measure represents is.
distractors.C: A genuine refinement, and worth doing — excluding intents the assistant cannot serve makes the number comparable across releases. But it repairs the denominator, not the incentive: a per-intent containment target is still satisfied by a chat the customer abandoned unhelped.

explanation.concept: Test every proposed success metric by asking how it could be maximised by a system that does not solve the problem. Any metric that counts an absence — no transfer, no escalation, no complaint — is gameable and must be paired with a positive outcome measure observed over a window long enough for the failure to reappear.
explanation.tip: One number is planted here and it decides the item: the repeat-contact rate is observed evidence that containment and resolution have diverged. Denominator refinements are worth doing but leave the incentive untouched, so they cannot be the most serious defect.

topic: Eliciting tone requirements a stakeholder cannot articulate
stem: A wealth management firm wants Claude to draft annual client review letters. The head of client experience insists the letters must 'sound like us' but cannot state any rule, and rejects sample drafts on instinct. Which TWO elicitation moves are most likely to yield a specifiable requirement? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Collect twenty letters she considers exemplary and ten she rejects, and have her mark the passages that drove each judgement.
Ask her to complete the brand team's tone questionnaire, scoring the desired voice on twenty adjective scales from formal to warm.
Derive a style guide from the firm's public marketing website and prospectus, and ask her to approve it as the drafting standard.
Produce three deliberately different drafts of the same real client letter and have her choose between them and annotate why.
Defer tone to a post-launch adviser feedback loop, on the basis that a subjective voice cannot be specified in advance.

explanation.correct: Both moves replace introspection with discrimination, which is the thing the stakeholder can actually do reliably. Marked-up exemplars and rejects give paired positive and negative evidence, and the marked passages convert instinct into citable features — hedging, sign-off form, how performance is described in a down year. Forced choice between deliberate variants isolates one dimension at a time and produces the same evidence prospectively. Both outputs are directly usable: exemplars become few-shot material and the annotations become rubric lines in the evaluation.

distractors.B: Adjective scales produce words like 'warm' and 'professional' that every firm selects and that no reviewer can apply consistently. The output cannot be turned into a check anyone could grade the drafts against.
distractors.C: Wrong corpus. Marketing voice is written to attract prospects; an adviser's review letter to an existing client under a fiduciary relationship reads nothing like it. It also asks for approval of an artefact she did not generate, which produces polite agreement rather than information.
distractors.E: Abandons a requirement that is specifiable by other means and defers all the rework to after launch, when the reviewers are the advisers whose confidence in the tool is being established.

explanation.concept: When a stakeholder cannot state a rule, stop asking for the rule. Collect judgements on concrete artefacts — exemplars, rejects and forced choices — and infer the rule from the boundary between them. Negative examples carry more information than positive ones, because they mark where the acceptable region ends.
explanation.tip: In elicitation items, prefer options that ask the stakeholder to judge something concrete over options that ask them to describe something abstract. Anything that produces adjectives is a distractor.

topic: Retargeting a request when the baseline leaves no headroom
stem: A regional airline's crew planning team asks for Claude to check crew duty-time legality. A deterministic rules engine performs this today and has produced no legality breach in three years of operation. The team's stated frustration is that when the engine rejects a roster, its coded messages are unintelligible to crew and planners, generating around 40 support calls a week. What should qualification conclude?

options.text: Re-target at the real pain — turning rejection codes and the relevant rule text into plain language — and leave legality with the engine.
Have the model re-check every roster the engine passes, running in parallel as an independent second opinion on duty-time legality.
Replace the rules engine so a single system both determines duty-time legality and explains its reasoning in natural language.
Decline the request; generating explanations is presentational polish and does not justify funding a delivery programme.

explanation.correct: Three years without a breach means the determination has no headroom worth buying, and the stated pain is not in the determination at all — it is 40 calls a week caused by unreadable output. Explanation over a structured input with a known correct answer is a strong model fit: the ground truth already exists, the failure mode is mild, and the value is measurable in support call volume. Qualification's job here is to separate the part of the request that is already solved from the part that is not.

distractors.B: Buys a second opinion on a determination with a three-year perfect record, and creates a new problem: what the operation does when the two disagree. Almost every disagreement will be the model being wrong, and adjudicating them costs more than the calls.
distractors.C: Trades a deterministic, auditable, provably reliable control for a probabilistic one in a safety-regulated domain, in exchange for a benefit that can be obtained without touching the engine at all.
distractors.D: Reads 'explanation' as cosmetic and misses that the stem quantifies the cost — 40 support calls a week is a measurable outcome with a clear baseline, which makes this one of the easier value cases to prove.

explanation.concept: Before accepting a use case as stated, locate where the cost actually is. When an existing deterministic component performs its job correctly, the opportunity is usually adjacent to it — explaining, translating, triaging or preparing its input — rather than replacing it. Perfect incumbent accuracy is a signal to move the target, not to compete.
explanation.tip: A stem that reports a long clean record for the existing system is telling you accuracy is not the opportunity. Read the sentence describing what people actually complain about; that is where the answer is.

topic: Elements of a usable discovery problem statement
stem: Discovery produces a short problem statement for each qualified use case. Which set of elements makes that statement usable as the basis for both design and acceptance?

options.text: The competitive landscape, the vendor shortlist and the procurement route through the group framework agreement.
The sponsor's name, the cost-centre budget code and the target go-live quarter in the portfolio plan.
Who decides today, which inputs they use, what output they produce, how often, and the cost of getting it wrong.
The chosen model tier, the integration pattern and the estimated monthly run cost at forecast call volume.

explanation.correct: Each element does specific downstream work. Naming the current decision-maker identifies who to elicit from and who is affected. Inputs define the retrieval and context problem and expose whether the information is even accessible. The output defines the interface contract. Frequency drives volume, cost and latency requirements. And the consequence of error sets the autonomy level, the guardrails and the human-in-the-loop placement. A statement with all five can be designed against and tested against; one missing the error consequence is the most common defect.

distractors.A: Procurement artefacts. They may be needed to buy something, but they contain no description of the problem, so no design or acceptance criterion can be derived from them.
distractors.B: Governance metadata. It records who owns the work and when it is due without stating what the work is, which is precisely what the design team needs.
distractors.D: Solution decisions rather than a problem statement. Recording them at this point fixes the answer before the problem is described, and they will change as soon as the real constraints surface.

explanation.concept: A problem statement is complete when it constrains the design. Actor, inputs, output, frequency and consequence-of-error each map to a specific architectural decision. Write them before any solution language enters the document, and the error consequence in particular, because it determines how much autonomy the system may be given.
explanation.tip: Options full of solution nouns — model tier, integration pattern, vendor — are answering a later question. Problem statements contain no technology.

topic: Discovery finding that the binding constraint is source data quality
stem: A pharmaceutical distributor wants Claude to answer field representatives' product availability questions from the ERP. During discovery the architect runs 80 real questions directly against the ERP: in 34 of them the ERP stock figure differs from the warehouse's own physical count by more than 10%. The reconciliation gap is known internally and has no owner. The sponsor wants a working prototype in three weeks. What is the best next step?

options.text: Build the prototype on the ERP stock figures and attach a standing disclaimer to every answer that availability is indicative rather than guaranteed.
Take the finding to the sponsor as a precondition: either the reconciliation gap gets an owner and a remediation date, or availability drops out of scope.
Add retrieval over the warehouse physical-count system so the assistant reconciles the two figures at answer time and reports any discrepancy to the rep.
Lower the accuracy acceptance threshold for availability answers so that it sits under the known ERP data-quality ceiling and the gate can be cleared.

explanation.correct: The measurement is the deliverable. A model reading a wrong number returns a wrong answer with new fluency and new reach — reps will trust it more than they trusted the screen, and the distributor's exposure rises. This is not a modelling problem and no prompt fixes it, so the decision belongs to the sponsor, framed as a choice between funding an owner for the reconciliation gap and cutting availability from scope. Discovery earns its keep precisely by surfacing this before three weeks of build make the commitment feel irreversible.

distractors.A: A disclaimer transfers liability on paper while the operational harm stands: a rep quoting an indicative figure to a customer still causes a failed order. It also cements the unowned data defect as permanent, since nobody will fund a fix once the tool is live.
distractors.C: Superficially the engineer's fix, but reconciling two disagreeing sources at answer time requires a rule deciding which is authoritative, and no one in the organisation has made that decision. The system would be inventing a business rule under a service-level constraint.
distractors.D: Moves the acceptance bar to accommodate a defect outside the system rather than reporting the defect. The resulting criterion certifies a system that is knowingly wrong at a rate the business never agreed to.

explanation.concept: Test the source data against reality during discovery, not the model against the source data. Where the upstream record is wrong, an assistant amplifies the error and raises its credibility. Findings of this kind must be escalated as a scope-or-remediate decision for the sponsor, because neither option is the architect's to take.
explanation.tip: When a stem tells you a data-quality gap is 'known but unowned', it is signalling that the answer involves giving it an owner or cutting the scope that depends on it — never engineering around it silently.

topic: Staging scope from read-only before granting write actions
stem: A property management company wants an assistant that answers tenant queries and can also cancel or reschedule contractor appointments in the scheduling system. Discovery establishes that a cancellation is irreversible in that system: the slot returns to the contractor's open pool and is often taken within minutes, and cancellations inside 24 hours also incur a contractor fee. The sponsor wants both capabilities in phase one. What scope should discovery recommend?

options.text: Include both, with a confirmation question quoting the appointment date to the tenant before any cancellation is executed.
Include both, but permit write actions only on appointments more than 24 hours away, where no contractor fee applies.
Include both, and log every write action with its triggering transcript so mistakes can be identified and put right the next day.
Ship read-only in phase one and gate write actions on phase-one evidence that the assistant reads reschedule intent correctly.

explanation.correct: The action is irreversible and there is currently no evidence about how often the assistant would read a tenant's intent correctly. Phase one generates exactly that evidence at zero risk: the assistant classifies intent and proposes an action while a human executes, so every proposal becomes a labelled case. The gate is then an empirical one against real traffic rather than a judgement made before launch. This also delivers the query-answering value on the sponsor's timeline, so the staging costs nothing except the write capability nobody can yet justify.

distractors.A: A tenant asked to confirm cannot tell whether the assistant selected the right appointment, the right property or the right contractor. Confirmation is a meaningful control only when the confirming party can verify the thing being confirmed.
distractors.B: Removes the fee but not the irreversibility — a slot released more than 24 hours out is still gone within minutes, and re-booking may take weeks. It also mistakes the cost of the error for the risk, which is a wrong cancellation of any kind.
distractors.C: Detection after the fact. Logging is necessary and should be built regardless, but an audit trail identifies which appointments were destroyed; it does not restore them, and the stem states restoration is not possible.

explanation.concept: Grant write access on evidence, not on intention. A read-only or propose-only first phase produces the labelled data that justifies autonomy, while irreversibility of the action — not its frequency or its unit cost — sets how much evidence is required before the gate opens.
explanation.tip: Scan the stem for the word irreversible or its equivalents. When an action cannot be undone, options offering detection, confirmation by an unqualified party, or a narrower blast radius are all weaker than staging the capability.

topic: Required properties of the acceptance evaluation set
stem: An acceptance evaluation set is agreed at the end of discovery and will decide whether the system is signed off. Which TWO properties must it have for that decision to be defensible? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: It contains only cases the current human process handles correctly, so the comparison is fair to the system.
It is frozen and withheld before prompt development begins, so no case in it shaped how the system was built.
It is generated by the model itself from the requirements, to maximise coverage of edge cases nobody thought of.
It contains an equal number of cases in every category, regardless of how often each one occurs in production.
Its case mix reflects the production distribution, including the exception classes discovery identified.

explanation.correct: Independence and representativeness are the two properties that make an acceptance number mean anything. If the set was visible during prompt development, the score measures fit to those cases rather than capability, and the gap only appears in production. If the mix does not match live traffic, the number is arithmetically unrelated to the experience users will have — a set overweighted with easy cases certifies a system that fails on the traffic that matters. Everything else about the set is a refinement of these two.

distractors.A: Excludes exactly the cases where the human process struggles, which are often where the system is most needed and most likely to fail. It manufactures a favourable score and hides the risk the sign-off is supposed to expose.
distractors.C: Model-generated cases inherit the generator's blind spots and its idea of what an edge case looks like. Synthetic data has a place in stress testing, but an acceptance set must be independent of the system it judges.
distractors.D: Balanced sets are a legitimate diagnostic tool for per-class performance, since rare classes otherwise have too few cases to say anything about. They are the wrong basis for an aggregate acceptance figure, because that figure then describes traffic that does not exist.

explanation.concept: An acceptance set must be frozen before build and distributed like production. Keep a separate, deliberately balanced diagnostic set if you need per-class visibility, but never let it be the set the threshold is applied to. Agreeing both sets during discovery, while nobody yet knows which cases are hard, is what keeps the eventual sign-off honest.
explanation.tip: For eval-set items, check two things only: was it hidden from the builders, and does its mix look like production. Options about size, balance or generation method are usually secondary.

topic: Signals that a request is a process problem not a model problem
stem: A hospital trust asks for Claude to 'reduce the time clinicians spend on discharge summaries'. Which THREE discovery findings would indicate that the request is primarily a process or data problem rather than a language model problem? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: Time-and-motion sampling shows most elapsed time is spent waiting for pharmacy to confirm the medication list, not composing text.
Consultants dictate summaries in free text, and phrasing, ordering and section headings vary widely between individual consultants and specialties.
The summary's content sits in three systems, one reachable only through a nightly export that lands after most discharges have happened.
The record system already auto-populates the summary, and the real complaint is re-keying the same content into a separate GP portal.
Junior doctors report the hardest part is judging which findings from a long admission are clinically relevant to the receiving GP.

explanation.correct: Each of the three locates the cost somewhere a model cannot reach. A waiting-time bottleneck is a dependency between two teams, and generating text faster shortens a step that was not the constraint. A source that only becomes available after the event is a data-availability and scheduling defect: at the moment the summary is written the information does not exist to be summarised. And a re-keying complaint describes an integration gap between two systems that already hold the content, which an interface solves and a generative step does not.

distractors.B: Variation in individual phrasing over free-text dictation is the textbook case for a model: normalising heterogeneous natural language into a consistent structured output is what it is good at. This finding supports the use case rather than undermining it.
distractors.E: Deciding which findings are clinically relevant to a particular reader is judgement over unstructured clinical narrative, guided by policy that no decision table captures. This is the strongest argument in the list for a model, with human review retained.

explanation.concept: Before accepting a time-saving use case, find where the time actually goes. Waiting, re-keying and unavailable data are process and integration defects, and automating the composition step around them saves the smallest part of the total. Only the portion of elapsed time spent on interpretation or generation is addressable by a model.
explanation.tip: In a list of findings, sort each into 'the model would do this work' versus 'the model would wait for someone else to finish'. The second kind is a process problem no matter how the request was phrased.

topic: Composing the attendee list for a discovery workshop
stem: A council has two hours for a discovery workshop on automating disabled-parking-badge application assessment. Invited so far: the service manager, two team leaders, the IT business partner and a supplier account manager. Which addition would most improve what the session produces?

options.text: Two assessors who process applications daily, with ten recent applications including two refusals.
The council's chief executive, to signal senior commitment and unblock the programme's funding at cabinet.
The supplier's solution architect, to set out the integration and licensing options available for the platform.
A member of the communications team, to begin planning the public announcement to existing badge holders.

explanation.correct: Nobody currently invited assesses applications. Team leaders describe the process they manage; only the assessors hold the rules they actually apply, particularly on refusals, where the reasoning is least documented and the appeal risk is highest. Bringing real applications turns the session from recollection into inspection — the group works through cases rather than abstractions, and the refused ones expose the decision boundary. Two hours spent this way produces requirements and the beginnings of an evaluation set at the same time.

distractors.B: Senior attendance changes what people say. Operators are less likely to describe workarounds and exceptions in front of a chief executive, which removes precisely the content the workshop exists to capture.
distractors.C: Technical options presented before the problem is understood anchor the group on a solution shape. The supplier architect is valuable later; in a two-hour discovery slot they consume time that belongs to the problem.
distractors.D: Announcement planning presupposes a decision that has not been taken. It is out of phase and would displace attendees who hold the information the session needs.

explanation.concept: A discovery workshop needs the people who perform the work, not only those who manage or enable it, and it needs real artefacts in the room. Refused, escalated and exception cases carry far more information per minute than descriptions of the standard path, because that is where undocumented judgement lives.
explanation.tip: When an invitation list is given, look for whether anyone in it actually does the task. Senior attendance and supplier presence are usually the distractors — they change the conversation without adding knowledge of the work.

topic: Conflicting requirements from two co-funding business units
stem: An insurer's discovery for a claims-note summariser surfaces a conflict between the two units co-funding it. Claims operations want summaries under 100 words so handlers can read them at pace across a high caseload. The fraud team wants every inconsistency between the claimant's statements preserved, which on contested claims runs past 400 words. Contested claims are about 6% of volume. How should discovery resolve this?

options.text: Set a single 250-word cap on every summary as a compromise both the claims and the fraud team can sign up to.
Specify two outputs from one analysis pass: a short handler summary and a separate flagged-inconsistency record for fraud.
Escalate to the joint sponsor to rule on which unit's requirement takes precedence in the summary specification.
Adopt the fraud requirement throughout, since the regulatory exposure from a missed inconsistency outweighs handler reading time.

explanation.correct: The requirements only conflict if you assume one artefact. They are describing different consumers, different moments and different decisions: a handler triaging at volume, and a fraud analyst investigating 6% of cases in depth. One analysis pass can emit both, and separating them lets each be measured against its own criterion — brevity and sufficiency for the handler, recall of inconsistencies for fraud. Discovery's contribution is spotting that the apparent trade-off is an artefact of the assumed output format.

distractors.A: A midpoint that satisfies neither requirement: too long to read at caseload pace, too short to preserve the inconsistencies fraud needs. Splitting the difference on a genuine conflict of purpose produces an output with no satisfied consumer.
distractors.C: Escalating a resolvable design question spends sponsor attention and produces a loser who was co-funding the work. Escalation is for genuine value conflicts, not for conflicts created by an unexamined assumption about the deliverable.
distractors.D: Imposes the needs of 6% of claims on all of them, adding reading time to every case a handler touches. It also mistakes preserving detail for detecting fraud; the fraud team needs flagged inconsistencies, not longer prose.

explanation.concept: When two stakeholders demand opposite properties of one output, check whether they are actually the same consumer. Different consumers with different decisions usually justify different views over shared analysis, and separating the views converts an unwinnable negotiation into a design decision with two clean acceptance criteria.
explanation.tip: A conflict where both sides are obviously right about their own job is a signal that the unit of delivery is wrong. Look for the assumption that there must be one output.

topic: Reversibility rather than difficulty as the autonomy gate
stem: A business energy supplier is qualifying two candidate actions for an assistant that acts on customer requests end to end. One is emailing a duplicate copy of an invoice. The other is initiating a supplier switch, which under market rules opens a regulated objection window and, once it completes unopposed, can only be undone by a fresh switch taking several weeks. Both actions have similar request volume, and the intent-classification task for each is of comparable difficulty. What should qualification decide?

options.text: Both qualify equally for autonomous execution, since request volume and intent-classification difficulty are the same for each action.
Neither qualifies for autonomous execution until intent classification is demonstrated above 99% on a held-out set of real requests.
Invoice reissue can execute autonomously; switch initiation needs explicit customer confirmation and a staff-reversible hold before submission.
Both qualify provided every action is written to an immutable log alongside the transcript that triggered it, giving a full audit trail for disputes.

explanation.correct: The stem deliberately equalises volume and classification difficulty so that only one variable is left. A wrongly reissued invoice costs a customer thirty seconds of confusion and is trivially undone; a wrongly initiated switch moves a business customer's supply, breaches trust, and takes weeks and a second market transaction to unwind. Autonomy should be priced against the cost of being wrong, not against how often you expect to be. That yields different controls for the two actions even though the model's task is identical.

distractors.A: Treats the two actions as interchangeable because their inputs look alike. It is the exact reasoning error the item is testing: classification difficulty describes how often you will be wrong, not what happens when you are.
distractors.B: Applies one blanket threshold to actions with very different consequences, which over-controls the harmless action and under-controls the harmful one. A single accuracy bar is also the wrong instrument, because no achievable rate makes an unrecoverable action safe on its own.
distractors.D: Audit logging supports dispute handling and is worth building, but it records that a switch was initiated in error rather than preventing or reversing it. Detection is not a control for an action the stem states cannot be undone quickly.

explanation.concept: Set the autonomy level of each action from the reversibility and blast radius of its worst outcome, evaluated action by action rather than system-wide. Two actions in the same assistant can legitimately sit at different autonomy levels, and holding a reversible hold before an irreversible external transaction is usually cheaper than any accuracy improvement.
explanation.tip: When a stem equalises every variable except one, the equalised ones are noise. Here volume and difficulty are held constant precisely so that consequence is the only thing left to reason from.

topic: Late-surfacing integration constraint on the submitting actor
stem: In week eight of a nine-week discovery at a freight forwarder, with the design nearly signed off, a customs subject matter expert mentions that any automated customs declaration must be lodged through the national customs gateway, which accepts a specific XML schema and authenticates with a per-individual digital certificate held by each operations clerk. No service credential exists in the scheme as far as anyone present knows. The value case assumed end-to-end automated lodgement. What is the best next step?

options.text: Record certificate and schema handling as an implementation detail in the build backlog, and sign the design off on the agreed week-nine date.
Redesign around a shared service account and open a formal request with the national customs authority to have one issued before the build starts.
Permanently remove customs lodgement from scope and deliver only the internal booking and documentation parts of the workflow.
Re-open feasibility on lodgement alone: check whether a non-individual credential exists, and if not, make the clerk the lodging actor and re-cost.

explanation.correct: An authentication model that binds submissions to a named individual is not an implementation detail; it decides whether the workflow can be automated end to end or is inherently assisted. That distinction changes the value case, because a clerk reviewing and lodging each declaration saves a different amount of time from a system lodging them unattended. The correct move is a narrow, fast feasibility check on that one step, followed by re-costing — which is a few days of work, not a re-run of discovery.

distractors.A: Signs off a design whose central assumption may be false. If no service credential exists, the build team discovers in sprint two that the automation the business case promised cannot be built, at far greater cost than a week of checking now.
distractors.B: Commits to a design premised on an external regulator changing its access model, on a timeline nobody controls. Requesting a service credential is worth doing in parallel, but it cannot be the plan of record for a week-nine sign-off.
distractors.C: Jumps to the pessimistic outcome before the question has been asked. Permanent descoping also throws away the assisted-lodgement shape, which may still carry most of the value with the clerk in the loop.

explanation.concept: A constraint that determines who the acting party is changes the value case, not just the build. When one surfaces late, run a narrow feasibility check on that step and re-cost the benefit under the assisted variant, rather than absorbing it as a detail or abandoning the scope outright.
explanation.tip: Per-individual credentials, wet signatures and named-person approvals are all signals that a human must remain the actor. Treat them as value-case constraints, not integration chores.

topic: Characteristics indicating a genuine language model fit
stem: Which TWO characteristics most reliably indicate that a task belongs to a language model rather than to deterministic rules or a classical statistical model? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The task produces a numeric value that must be reproducible to the penny whenever an auditor asks.
The task runs at very high volume on inputs arriving in a fixed schema that has not changed in years.
Inputs arrive as natural language or documents and vary in ways nobody can enumerate in advance.
The organisation already holds a large, cleanly labelled training set covering the task's categories.
The output requires judgement that written policy describes but no decision table can capture.

explanation.correct: These are the two conditions under which rule-writing fails for reasons no amount of engineering effort fixes. Unenumerable input variation means every rule set is incomplete the moment it ships, and maintaining it costs more each year. Policy-guided judgement means the correct answer depends on reading and weighing prose that resists tabulation — the case an expert handles by reference to the policy rather than by lookup. Where both hold, a model earns its cost and its non-determinism; where neither holds, it rarely does.

distractors.A: The clearest signal for the opposite conclusion. Exact reproducible arithmetic is what deterministic code guarantees and a probabilistic system does not, and auditors will ask for the code path rather than the prompt.
distractors.B: Fixed schema at very high volume argues for rules or a small purpose-built classifier. Stability removes the variation that justifies a general model, and volume magnifies the per-call cost difference.
distractors.D: A large clean labelled set is the classic precondition for supervised learning, which will usually be cheaper and faster to serve at scale for a well-defined task. It is a reason to consider a trained classifier, not a reason to reach for a general model.

explanation.concept: Qualify on input variability and on whether the decision rule is tabulatable. Unenumerable natural-language input plus policy-guided judgement is the combination that defeats rules and classical models alike. Stable schemas, exact arithmetic and abundant labels all point elsewhere, and saying so is the fastest way to build credibility with a sceptical engineering audience.
explanation.tip: Availability of labelled data feels like it should favour the model, which is why it appears in these lists. It usually argues for the classical approach instead.

topic: Comparing against the best non-AI alternative
stem: Why should a discovery business case compare the proposed Claude system against the best available non-AI improvement to the same process, rather than only against the current state?

options.text: Measuring only against today's process credits the model with gains a cheaper process or integration fix would also deliver.
Financial regulators require a documented alternatives analysis to be filed with the supervisor before any AI system may be deployed.
It is the only reliable way to derive the latency and throughput budget the new system will have to meet in production.
Non-AI alternatives are almost always cheaper, so the comparison usually ends the project early and saves discovery time.

explanation.correct: The current state is a low bar that includes every inefficiency a form redesign, a queue change or a missing integration is responsible for. Attributing all of that improvement to the model inflates the return and, worse, makes the claim indefensible at the post-implementation review when someone points out the process changed too. Comparing against the strongest cheap alternative isolates the increment that genuinely requires a model, which is both the honest number and the one that survives challenge.

distractors.B: There is no general regulatory requirement of this kind, and framing it as compliance obscures the real reason. Some regimes require documented justification for particular high-risk uses, but that is not why this comparison belongs in every business case.
distractors.C: Latency budgets come from the consuming process and its service commitments. An alternatives comparison says nothing about how fast the system must respond.
distractors.D: Overstates the conclusion. Sometimes the cheap alternative does win, which is a good outcome, but often the comparison shows a real increment. Using the technique because you expect it to kill projects is not a reason to use it.

explanation.concept: Value claims must be incremental against the best realistic alternative, not absolute against the status quo. Ask what a competent team would achieve with process redesign, a report or an integration and no model at all; the model must be justified by the gap above that line, not by the whole distance from today.
explanation.tip: Any option that justifies a practice by invoking an unnamed regulatory requirement deserves suspicion. The real reason is usually about the integrity of the measurement.

topic: Choosing the second use case after a successful first build
stem: A specialty chemicals manufacturer runs one Claude system in production: question answering over a curated safety-data-sheet corpus, with a retrieval pipeline, an evaluation harness and a review workflow the regulatory function has accepted. Discovery has capacity for exactly one more build, and the programme must show value within one quarter to secure continuing funding. Candidates are: summarising customer complaint emails (new corpus, new consumers, highest volume); answering regulatory compliance questions over the same curated corpus for a different internal team; an autonomous agent that raises purchase orders; and a demand-forecasting capability. Which should be selected?

options.text: Complaint email summarisation, because it carries the highest volume of the four candidates and therefore the largest measurable time saving in the quarter.
Regulatory compliance questions over the same curated corpus, because the retrieval pipeline, evaluation harness and accepted review workflow all carry over.
The purchase order agent, because demonstrating autonomous action end to end makes the strongest case to the continuing-funding committee.
Demand forecasting, because broadening from language into predictive work widens the programme's remit and its future funding base.

explanation.correct: A one-quarter deadline makes reuse the dominant consideration. The compliance use case inherits the corpus, the retrieval and chunking decisions, the eval harness and — most valuably — a review workflow the regulatory function has already accepted, which is the asset that takes longest to rebuild because it is social rather than technical. What remains is a new question set, new evaluation cases and a new consumer group. Every other candidate spends most of the quarter re-establishing something this one already has.

distractors.A: Highest volume, but a new corpus, new consumers, new evaluation criteria and a new review relationship. Volume determines the size of the eventual prize, not whether it can be demonstrated inside a quarter with the capacity available.
distractors.C: Introduces autonomous write actions into procurement as a second-ever build, before the organisation has any operating experience with an agentic system. The risk profile and the approvals required make a one-quarter demonstration unlikely, and a visible failure here costs the whole programme.
distractors.D: Numeric extrapolation over structured history is not a language model problem in the first place, so this candidate should not have survived qualification. Choosing it also spends the quarter building capability the team does not have.

explanation.concept: After a first success, sequence the portfolio by asset reuse — corpus, retrieval, evaluation harness, guardrails and, above all, an accepted human review relationship — weighted by time to demonstrable value. The second build should extend proven ground; save new data domains and new autonomy levels for when the funding is no longer conditional.
explanation.tip: When a stem imposes a short window to prove value, rank the candidates by how much existing infrastructure and accumulated trust each one inherits. The highest-volume option is usually the distractor.

topic: Eliciting the real escalation boundary from case evidence
stem: A building society is scoping an assistant to handle mortgage arrears enquiries. Its vulnerable-customer policy instructs advisers to 'escalate where vulnerability is suspected' and gives illness, bereavement and job loss as examples. The architect must specify when the assistant hands off to a human. What is the most useful elicitation move?

options.text: Ask the compliance function to write an operational definition of vulnerability, with worked tests, that the assistant can apply directly to each call.
Configure the assistant to hand off whenever illness, bereavement or job loss is mentioned, mirroring the three examples the policy itself gives.
Have the assistant hand off whenever its own reported confidence in the arrears response falls below an agreed numeric threshold.
Review the last hundred escalations advisers raised with the recorded trigger, alongside comparable calls not escalated, and derive the boundary.

explanation.correct: The policy is deliberately open-textured, so the operating rule exists only in adviser practice. Escalated cases alone show what crosses the line but not where it is; the non-escalated comparison sample is what locates the boundary, and it also reveals disagreement between advisers, which is itself a finding the compliance function needs. The result is a specification grounded in behaviour the society can defend to its regulator, plus a labelled set of positive and negative cases that becomes the handoff evaluation.

distractors.A: Compliance definitions are written to be defensible and broad, which is why the existing one says 'suspected'. Asking for a tighter written definition usually returns another abstraction, and it puts compliance in the position of inventing a rule rather than ratifying observed practice.
distractors.B: Keyword triggers fail in both directions: vulnerability is often signalled obliquely — confusion, a third party speaking for the customer, an unexplained payment pattern — while a passing mention of a past illness escalates a call that needed no handoff.
distractors.C: The model's confidence in its answer is unrelated to whether the customer is vulnerable. It may be entirely confident about a payment holiday while missing every distress signal in the conversation, so this routes on the wrong quantity.

explanation.concept: Where policy is intentionally open-textured, elicit the operating rule from decided cases on both sides of the line. Positive examples alone define an inclusion set, never a boundary. Present the derived boundary back to the policy owner for ratification so the specification carries their authority rather than the architect's inference.
explanation.tip: Whenever an option routes on the model's own confidence, check whether confidence is even about the right quantity. Here it measures certainty about an answer, not the presence of a customer risk signal.
